description_full: Cognex Corporation provides machine vision products that capture and analyze visual information to automate manufacturing and distribution tasks in the United States, Europe, Greater China, and internationally. Its machine vision products are used to automate the manufacture and distribution of discrete items, such as mobile phones, automotive components, and e-commerce packages, by locating, identifying, inspecting, and measuring them. The company offers VisionPro software, a suite of patented vision tools for traditional rule-based tools and deep learning-enabled tools for advanced programming; vision systems that combine smart cameras and software to perform a wide range of tasks, including part location, identification, measurement, assembly verification, and robotic guidance; OneVision, a cloud-based platform designed to transform how manufacturers build, train, and scale AI-powered vision applications; In-Sight product line of vision systems and sensors; QuickBuild, which allows customers to build vision applications with a graphical and flowchart-based programming interface; DataMan, an image-based barcode reader for fixed-mount and handheld models, as well as barcode verifiers; and vision accessories, such as industrial cameras, lenses, lighting, vision controllers, frame grabbers, and I/O cards. It sells its products to the automotive, logistics, packaging, consumer electronics, medical-related, semiconductor, and consumer products industries. The company was incorporated in 1981 and is headquartered in Natick, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Cognex Corporation is a mid-cap technology business with a $8.0B market cap on $994M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 74% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $237M in free cash flow — roughly 24 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 9pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.70x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-15.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 69% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 29% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 59% and a beta of 1.20, it moves roughly with the market.
About $99.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 49% in the 2022 bear market and 65% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $31.93 (margin of safety -50%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 34%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $22.80 to $46.21 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: EV/EBITDA 23.7 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 34.0 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 27% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 19 covering analysts target $79.37 on average, 66% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.36).
It runs a 74% gross margin and converts 24% of revenue into free cash flow, or 19% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.15x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 14.0% of revenue on R&D and 4.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $337.0M (3% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 10.5, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 151 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.4% over 3 years, 4.2% over 5 years and 8.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 57% of profits supports about 5.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 0.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 23, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (31 sales, net $19.2M sold).
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (1.9% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 11 consecutive years, though it has been cut 32.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 2,745 employees, each generates about $362K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and productivity has risen 8.5% a year.
That works out to $86K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.6M (4x revenue per employee).
